# optimizers7 <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="" />

Almost every R package that fits a model carries its own optimizer, written
inside the function that needs it: a loop, a `while (!converged)`, a tolerance
compared with a quantity chosen by the author. Such an optimizer cannot be
reused or extended outside the package, and it provides only the quantities
that its author needed. The stopping rule, which defines what the procedure
means by *finished*, is usually a constant deep inside the code.

In `{optimizers7}`, each optimizer is written once, as an object. An
optimizer carries its algorithm and every setting of that algorithm; a
stopping rule is a separate object that can be replaced, combined, or written
by the user; and every algorithm is written once against one interface for
the objective.

The package minimizes the function that it is given, and it does not
represent observations, the origin of the data or the meaning of the
parameters. Those belong to the calling package.

It is the optimization layer of [statmodels7](https://statmodels7.github.io),
alongside [linkfunctions7](https://statmodels7.github.io/linkfunctions7/) and
[distributions7](https://statmodels7.github.io/distributions7/).

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("statmodels7/optimizers7")
```

To install the whole toolkit, including the other packages of the toolkit,
use:

```{r eval=FALSE}
pak::pak("statmodels7/statmodels7")
```

## Minimizing a function

Every algorithm minimizes, through one generic:

```{r}
f  <- function(p) 100 * (p[2] - p[1]^2)^2 + (1 - p[1])^2
gr <- function(p) c(-400 * p[1] * (p[2] - p[1]^2) - 2 * (1 - p[1]),
                    200 * (p[2] - p[1]^2))

minimize(bfgs(), f, par = c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)
```

Changing the algorithm changes one word, because every optimizer carries the
same shared settings:

```{r}
minimize(lbfgs(), f, c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)@par
minimize(newton(), f, c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)@par
minimize(nelder_mead(), f, c(-1.2, 1))@par
```

## Stopping rules

A rule written inside an algorithm fixes the meaning of convergence when the
package is written. Here a rule is an object:

```{r}
crit_any(crit_grad(1e-10), crit_rel_obj(1e-14))
```

Rules compose, and a new rule is one class and one method:

```{r}
CritTiny <- S7::new_class("CritTiny", parent = criterion,
                          properties = list(tol = S7::class_numeric))
S7::method(crit_met, CritTiny) <- function(criterion, state)
  state$f_new < criterion@tol

minimize(bfgs(criterion = CritTiny(label = "f < 1e-8", tol = 1e-8)),
         f, c(-1.2, 1), gr = gr)@criterion_met
```

A rule that an optimizer cannot evaluate is rejected when the run starts,
with an error that names the missing quantity, instead of being accepted and
never firing:

```{r, error = TRUE}
minimize(nelder_mead(criterion = crit_grad()), f, c(-1.2, 1))
```

## Bounds by reparametrization

Each bounded coordinate is reparametrized onto the whole real line, so every
proposed point is admissible by construction: there is no rejection step and
no boundary for a line search to cross, and a method needs no code of its own
for bounds. The exception is `prox_grad()`, which takes its constraint through
its proximal operator and rejects `lower` and `upper`:

```{r}
y <- rnorm(200, mean = 0, sd = 2)
nll <- function(p) length(y) * log(p) + sum(y^2) / (2 * p^2)

minimize(bfgs(), nll, par = 1, lower = 0)@par
sqrt(mean(y^2))
```

## Starting values that need not be written out

`par` may be a starter instead of a vector. Both starters work on the
*unconstrained* scale and are mapped back through the bounds. On that scale
one constant suits every kind of parameter, since zero becomes one for a
variance and one half for a probability, and every draw lies inside its
box:

```{r}
X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(60), 30))
b <- drop(X %*% c(0.5, -1, 2)) + rnorm(30, sd = 0.2)
rss <- function(p) sum((b - X %*% p)^2)

minimize(bfgs(), rss, start_zeros())@par        # how many? worked out
minimize(bfgs(), rss, start_runif(-2, 2))@par   # or drawn, on that scale
```

The number of parameters is given by `start_zeros(npar = 3)`, by bounds with
one element per parameter, or, as above, by the objective itself, probed once
before the run. `X %*% p` with a parameter of the wrong length is an error
and not a number, so an objective written as a matrix product determines the
length. A vectorized expression that accepts several lengths does not, and
the probe then raises an error that names the lengths accepted.

## Objectives without a derivative at the minimum

A descent method reaches the minimum of a sum of absolute deviations and
then reports that it did not converge. The report is correct, because the
subgradient that it evaluates near the minimum has norm 1 and does not
become small. `bundle()` keeps a *collection* of subgradients and tests
whether zero lies in their convex hull, which is the condition that holds at
the minimizer:

```{r}
z <- rnorm(101)
sad <- function(p) sum(abs(z - p))
sub <- function(p) -sum(sign(z - p))

c(bfgs   = minimize(bfgs(), sad, par = 0, gr = sub)@converged,
  bundle = minimize(bundle(), sad, par = 0, gr = sub)@converged)

c(bundle = minimize(bundle(), sad, par = 0, gr = sub)@par, median = median(z))
```

## Components of the package

| | |
|---|---|
| second order | `newton()`, `bfgs()`, `lbfgs()` |
| third order | `chebyshev()` |
| first order | `cg()`, `bb()`, `gd()` |
| noisy objectives, and long parameter vectors | `adam()` |
| no derivative | `nelder_mead()`, `compass()` |
| one parameter | `brent()` |
| global search | `sa()` |
| non-smooth, with subgradients | `bundle()` |
| non-smooth, with a proximal operator | `prox_grad()` |
| wrappers | `multistart()`, parallel by default, and `chain()` |
| line searches | `armijo()`, `wolfe()`, `nonmonotone()` |
| starting values | `start_zeros()`, `start_runif()` |
| stopping rules | `crit_grad()`, `crit_abs_obj()`, `crit_rel_obj()`, `crit_abs_par()`, `crit_rel_par()`, `crit_stationary()`, `crit_never()`, and `crit_any()` / `crit_all()` to combine them |

Every method counts its own evaluations, records in its trace the
safeguards that fired, and sets `converged` only when the run ended on its
stopping rule (or on the resolution of the objective), never because a
budget ran out.

`multistart()` runs its starts in parallel without any setup: `cores` is a
number, by default as many processes as there are starts and at most the
number of cores minus two. The call itself starts the workers, loads the
package on them, gives each of them an independent random stream and shuts
them down. The implementation uses forks on Linux and macOS and a
socket cluster on Windows. For a deterministic optimizer such as `bfgs()`,
`set.seed()` reproduces the run identically however many cores were used;
for a stochastic one such as `sa()` the result depends on `cores`.

## Validating an optimizer

`check_optimizer()` runs twelve checks on what an optimizer reports: that
`value` is the objective at `par`, that a reported gradient is the gradient
there, that bounds hold *strictly*, that a run repeats, and others. It then
reports, separately, the gaps that the method reached on the standard test
problems; these gaps measure performance and do not enter the verdicts:

```{r}
check_optimizer(bfgs())
```
